title: Predicting Numbers
story: You run a snack cart. Each morning you read two numbers, (i) the sunshine score and (ii) the rain score, and you must predict two quantities: ice cream sales and umbrella sales.
goal: One linear layer makes both predictions at once: the input row times the weight matrix, plus the bias row. Hover any connection or any matrix cell to light up its partners, and click a prediction to expand its arithmetic.
hint: The weight w₁₁ multiplies sunshine into the ice cream prediction; because sunshine drives ice cream sales, that weight is large and positive.
note: Illustrative numbers, chosen so that every product is easy to recompute by hand.
question: Why does the rain weight for ice creams sit below zero?
answer: Because rain lowers ice cream sales, its weight is negative: every unit of rain subtracts 3 from the prediction. This is linear regression, where each prediction is a weighted sum of the features plus a bias.

check.cellsMsg: Requirement: hover every weight (all 4 cells or edges) to trace each connection.

title: Choosing a Class
story: A sorting machine sees two numbers for each fruit, (i) a roundness score and (ii) a yellowness score, and must decide: apple or banana?
goal: The same linear layer now produces one score per class, and the larger score wins (that pick is called argmax). Try both mystery fruits and trace how the weights vote.
hint: Yellowness carries a large positive weight into the banana score, so a yellow fruit pushes that score up fast.
note: Illustrative scores; a real sorter would read such features from a camera.
question: What changed between predicting sales and choosing a fruit?
answer: The arithmetic is identical; only the reading changed. Regression reads the outputs as quantities, while classification compares the scores and picks the class with the largest one.

title: Why Nonlinearity?
story: Stack two linear layers and hope for a smarter machine: the input passes through W¹ and b¹ to make h, then h passes through W² and b² to make the output.
goal: Follow the numbers: the two stacked layers compute exactly what one combined layer computes, because (xW¹+b¹)W²+b² = x(W¹W²)+(b¹W²+b²). Switch the ReLU activation on and watch the shortcut break.
hint: Hover a cell of the combined matrix W¹W² to see the W¹ row and the W² column it is built from.
note: Illustrative numbers; ReLU(v) keeps v when v is positive and returns 0 otherwise.
question: What does the activation function add that no weight matrix can?
answer: Without an activation, any stack of linear layers equals one linear layer, so depth adds nothing. The ReLU clips negative values (here h₁ = −3 becomes 0), and after that no single matrix reproduces the outputs.

title: Find the Weights
story: Three students report their study hours and sleep hours, and their exam scores are known. The right weights are unknown; you must find them.
goal: Adjust w₁, w₂, and the bias with the + and − buttons until the mean absolute error over all three students falls to 3 or below. Every prediction updates as you work.
hint: When every prediction runs low, raise the bias; when predictions grow too slowly with study hours, raise w₁.
note: Illustrative data; the scores follow a hidden linear recipe that integer weights can match exactly.
question: Hand tuning three numbers took a while. What does that suggest about a million weights?
answer: Hand search does not scale, because real models hold millions of weights. Gradient descent automates exactly what you just did: the error tells every weight which direction to move. Training Camp shows that loop running.

check.errorMsg: Requirement: bring the mean absolute error to 3 or below; it is now {err}.
